query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases and why catastrophic failure may occur? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, predicted observations relative to the starting-state baseline, applicable exposure boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: At elevated temperatures in oxidizing environments, the additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 FCC high-entropy alloy degrades because selective oxidation of the aluminum and titanium at grain boundaries produces a brittle, non-adherent oxide phase that causes localized stress concentrations, promotes microcrack initiation, and ultimately leads to catastrophic failure. In contrast, under reducing conditions, the suppressed oxidation minimizes these deleterious effects.
generation.material_initial_state: Additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy with a homogeneous high-entropy FCC matrix containing finely dispersed strengthening phases
generation.intervention: Controlled shift of the gas environment from oxidizing (high oxygen partial pressure) to reducing (low oxygen partial pressure) during high-temperature exposure
generation.conditions: Exposure at elevated temperatures (e.g., 700–850 °C) for a sustained period in atmospheres with well-defined oxygen content (oxidizing vs reducing gases)
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of brittle grain-boundary oxide phases (likely Al2O3 and TiO2) that are non-coherent with the FCC matrix
generation.mechanism: At high temperatures in the presence of oxygen, the more reactive elements (Al, Ti) preferentially oxidize at grain boundaries and near precipitate interfaces. The resulting oxide phases have mismatched thermal expansion and induce local stresses. Over time, these stresses lead to crack nucleation and propagation. Under reducing conditions, the oxidation rate is significantly lowered, thus retarding the accumulation of these detrimental oxides and preserving mechanical integrity.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples held in oxidizing atmospheres will exhibit significant grain-boundary oxide formation, increased microcrack density, and a notable reduction in creep strength or tensile ductility relative to the starting state. In reducing atmospheres, these detrimental features will be mitigated, delaying catastrophic failure relative to the oxidizing condition baseline.
generation.baseline: The alloy’s initial, homogenous microstructure and mechanical performance measured in an inert or low-oxygen environment
generation.boundary: Temperature range above approximately 700 °C and oxygen partial pressures high enough to promote rapid selective oxidation; below these conditions, oxidation is less severe and the degradation mechanism may not dominate
generation.uncertainty: The precise kinetics of oxide scale formation, the quantitative threshold oxygen partial pressure needed to trigger the catastrophic oxidation-induced failure, and the interplay with any concurrent internal reduction or phase instability phenomena remain uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare identical samples of the alloy and subject them to prolonged thermal exposure at ~750–850 °C in two different gas atmospheres: one with a high oxygen partial pressure (oxidizing environment) and one with a reducing gas (e.g., high-purity H2 or an inert gas with controlled low oxygen contamination). Compare the evolution of microstructure, the development of oxide phases at grain boundaries, and the mechanical properties (e.g., creep and tensile tests) over time.
measurements: High-resolution microscopy (SEM/TEM) to characterize oxide layer morphology and crack formation
X-ray diffraction (XRD) and energy-dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) for phase identification of oxides
Mechanical testing to measure reductions in tensile strength, creep rupture life, or ductility over exposure time
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If there is no statistically significant difference in oxide formation, grain-boundary degradation, and mechanical failure between samples in oxidizing versus reducing environments—even under conditions where oxygen availability is markedly different—then the hypothesis that selective oxidation governs degradation and catastrophic failure would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
The High Temperature Tensile and Creep Behaviors of High Entropy Superalloy

Abstract: AbstractThis article presents the high temperature tensile and creep behaviors of a novel high entropy alloy (HEA). The microstructure of this HEA resembles that of advanced superalloys with a high entropy FCC matrix and L12 ordered precipitates, so it is also named as “high entropy superalloy (HESA)”. The tensile yield strengths of HESA surpass those of the reported HEAs from room temperature to elevated temperatures; furthermore, its creep resistance at 982 °C can be compared to those of some Ni-based superalloys. Analysis on experimental results indicate that HESA could be strengthened by the low stacking-fault energy of the matrix, high anti-phase boundary energy of the strengthening precipitate, and thermally stable microstructure. Positive misfit between FCC matrix and precipitate has yielded parallel raft microstructure during creep at 982 °C, and the creep curves of HESA were dominated by tertiary creep behavior.
